title: Republicans Push Capital Gains Tax Cut as Midterm Strategy Divides the Party
excerpt: GOP lawmakers want to index capital gains to inflation to woo voters ahead of November, but the proposal faces opposition from the party's own top tax writer.
body:
• Republican senators are pushing to index capital gains to inflation, a move that would reduce tax bills when investors sell assets like stocks and real estate.
  • Senator Ted Cruz has discussed the proposal with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, but whether the Treasury can act without Congress remains legally uncertain.
  • The cost ranges from $170 billion over a decade for new purchases to nearly $1 trillion if applied retroactively, according to the Yale Budget Lab.
  • Ways and Means Chairman Jason Smith has dismissed the housing affordability argument as crafted by "clever lobbyists," exposing a rift within the GOP.

Republican lawmakers are weighing a capital gains tax cut as the party searches for ways to address voter anxiety about the cost of living ahead of November's midterm elections, according to Bloomberg.

The proposal centers on indexing capital gains to inflation, which would allow taxpayers to adjust the purchase price of an asset to account for rising prices before calculating taxable gains. The change would effectively shrink the taxable profit on long-held investments, reducing what sellers owe the Internal Revenue Service.

Cruz Leads the Push

Senator Ted Cruz of Texas has emerged as the proposal's most vocal champion, framing it as a direct response to inflation that accumulated during the Biden administration.

https://x.com/ResisttheMS/status/2087504369247981865

"It would be the biggest step we could do to counteract the massive inflation under Joe Biden and the Democrats and have a positive impact on affordability, particularly affordability of housing, between now and the midterms."

— Senator Ted Cruz, R-Texas

Cruz said he recently raised the idea with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent over breakfast. He and Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina have previously urged Bessent to bypass Congress and implement the change through executive action. In March, the two senators wrote to the Treasury Department making the case, and several House Republicans followed with their own letter days later.

Senate Finance Committee Chairman Mike Crapo said he "personally" supports the measure and that it would be among proposals considered if Republicans assemble a follow-up tax package this year.

Resistance From the Top Tax Writer

The proposal faces a significant obstacle in Ways and Means Chairman Jason Smith, the House's top Republican on tax policy. Smith has voiced skepticism about the proposal's purported housing benefits, while acknowledging that the Treasury has the "flexibility" to act unilaterally.

"I'm a fan of reduced tax rates, but my focus and priority is delivering for working families," Smith said. He dismissed arguments that indexing capital gains would improve housing affordability as a narrative crafted by "clever lobbyists."

The divide reflects a broader tension within the GOP over whether a second major tax package can be assembled before the midterms. Republicans have discussed compiling a follow-up to President Trump's 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act to signal economic action to voters, but the party has not coalesced around a legislative strategy or specific policies.

Cost and Political Risk

The fiscal cost of indexing depends on scope. If the change applies only to newly purchased assets, the Yale Budget Lab estimates it would cost approximately $170 billion over a decade. If applied retroactively to all existing assets, the cost would balloon to nearly $1 trillion over the same period.

The distributional effects pose a political problem. According to the Yale Budget Lab, the top 0.1 percent of earners would receive average tax cuts of roughly $350,000, while households in the bottom two income quintiles would see no benefit. Cruz argued that Democrats would attack any Republican tax proposal regardless of its structure.

Whether the Treasury Department could implement the change without congressional approval remains legally contested. A similar effort was considered and abandoned during the George H.W. Bush administration over concerns about legal challenges.

Housing Market Implications

Proponents argue indexing would help unlock the housing market by reducing the tax penalty for selling a home held for many years. Under current law, the capital gains exclusion for primary residence sales has remained at $250,000 for single filers and $500,000 for married couples since 1997, even as home prices have risen more than 260 percent.

Research from the University of Illinois Chicago suggests that if these caps had kept pace with inflation, they would now stand at approximately $660,000 and $1.32 million. Nearly 29 million households now have more home equity than the single-filer exclusion protects, according to a National Association of Realtors analysis.

The 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act left existing capital gains tax rates unchanged at 0 percent, 15 percent and 20 percent, depending on income. Long-term capital gains continue to be taxed at these preferential rates, with 2026 thresholds starting at $49,450 for singles and $98,900 for married couples filing jointly before the 15 percent rate applies.
